facts.fact_text: On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 4 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
The applicant and other women had gathered in the Ayios Georgios church, where a service was in progress.
The applicant was arrested and taken by bus to the so-called 'Pavlides Garage'.
During the journey to the 'Pavlides Garage', the applicant was subjected to assaults, beatings and gestures of a sexual nature by the officers who had detained her.
One of the women detainees, Mrs Vrahimi (application no. 16078/90), was seriously beaten at the 'Pavlides Garage'.
At about midnight the applicant was interrogated at the 'Pavlides Garage'.
The applicant's interrogation at the 'Pavlides Garage' took place in Greek.
The applicant lied when asked for details concerning the members of her family during the interrogation at the 'Pavlides Garage'.
The applicant was told to sign a statement in Turkish at the 'Pavlides Garage' but did not do so as she did not understand Turkish.
The applicant considered that signing the statement in Turkish would have been tantamount to recognising the 'TRNC'.
On the morning of 20 July 1989 the applicant was taken to court where she was remanded in custody for forty-eight hours.
The applicant was subsequently transferred to a prison outside Nicosia, where she was kept in a cell with another two women.
The applicant could not sleep at the prison outside Nicosia due to the severe pain from the blows she had received.
During the night at the prison outside Nicosia, the applicant and the other detainees were harassed by the guards and told that the long-term prisoners would rape them.
The toilets and showers at the prison outside Nicosia were filthy and had no doors so the guards could see the detainees bathing.
Essential means of hygiene were lacking at the prison outside Nicosia.
At night at the prison outside Nicosia, the guards continually picked out individual detainees for checks.
The Government alleged that the applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone and entering the area under Turkish-Cypriot control.

The Government alleged that the Turkish-Cypriot police intervened in the face of the manifest inability of the Greek-Cypriot authorities and the UN Force in Cyprus to contain the incursion and its possible consequences.
The Government alleged that no force was used against demonstrators who did not intrude into the 'TRNC' border area.

The Government alleged that in the case of demonstrators who were arrested for violating the border, no more force was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned.
The Government alleged that no one was ill-treated.
The Government alleged that it was possible that some of the demonstrators had hurt themselves in the confusion or in attempting to scale barbed wire or other fencing.

The Government alleged that had the Turkish police, or anyone else, assaulted or beaten any of the demonstrators, the UN Secretary General would no doubt have referred to this in his report to the Security Council.
The Government alleged that the applicant was charged, tried, found guilty and sentenced to a short term of imprisonment.
The Government alleged that the applicant pleaded not guilty but did not give evidence and declined to use the available judicial remedies.
The Government alleged that the applicant was asked if she required assistance from a lawyer registered in the 'TRNC', but refused and did not ask for legal representation.
The Government alleged that interpretation services were provided at the trial by qualified interpreters.
The Government alleged that all the proceedings were translated into Greek.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code defines an unlawful assembly as occurring where five or more persons assemble with intent to commit an offence, or, being assembled with intent to carry out some common purpose, conduct themselves in such a manner as to cause persons in the neighbourhood to fear that the persons so assembled will commit a breach of the peace, or will by such assembly needlessly and without any reasonable occasion provoke other persons to commit a breach of the peace.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that it is immaterial that the original assembly was lawful if, being assembled, the persons conduct themselves with a common purpose in such a manner as to cause persons in the neighbourhood to fear a breach of the peace.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that when an unlawful assembly has begun to execute the purpose for which it assembled by a breach of the peace and to the terror of the public, the assembly is called a riot and the persons assembled are said to be riotously assembled.
According to section 71 of the Cypriot Criminal Code, any person who takes part in an unlawful assembly is guilty of a misdemeanour and liable to imprisonment for one year.

Section 80 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that any person who carries in public without lawful occasion any offensive arm or weapon in such a manner as to cause terror to any person is guilty of a misdemeanour and is liable to imprisonment for two years, and his arms or weapons shall be forfeited.
According to section 82 of the Cypriot Criminal Code, it is an offence to carry a knife outside the home.

Chapter 155, section 14(1)(b) of the Cypriot Criminal Procedure Law states that any officer may, without warrant, arrest any person who commits in his presence any offence punishable with imprisonment.
Chapter 155, section 14(1)(c) of the Cypriot Criminal Procedure Law states that any officer may, without warrant, arrest any person who obstructs a police officer while in the execution of his duty.

Section 9 of Law No. 5/72 states that any person who enters a prohibited military area without authorisation, or by stealth, or fraudulently, shall be tried by a military court in accordance with the Military Offences Act, and those found guilty shall be punished.
Subsection 12(1) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that no person shall enter or leave the Colony except through an approved port.

Subsection 12(5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of subsections (1), (2), (3) or (4) of section 12 shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds or to both such imprisonment and fine.

The Government alleged that the demonstrators, supported by the Greek-Cypriot administration, were demanding that the 'Green Line' in Nicosia should be dismantled.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.

In his report of 7 December 1989 on the UN operations in Cyprus, the UN Secretary General stated that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.
According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by UNFICYP and destroyed an UNFICYP observation post.

According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the demonstrators broke through the line formed by UNFICYP soldiers and entered a former school complex where UNFICYP reinforcements regrouped to prevent them from proceeding further.

According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, a short while later Turkish-Cypriot police and security forces elements forced their way into the area and apprehended 111 persons, 101 of them women.

According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the Ayios Kassianos school complex is situated in the UN buffer zone, but the Turkish forces claim it to be on their side of the cease-fire line.

According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, under working arrangements with UNFICYP, the Turkish-Cypriot security forces had patrolled the Ayios Kassianos school grounds for several years within specific restrictions, and this patrolling had ceased altogether as part of the unmanning agreement implemented the previous May.

According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, in the afternoon of 21 July 1989, some 300 Greek Cypriots gathered at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia to protest the continuing detention by the Turkish-Cypriot authorities of those apprehended at Ayios Kassianos.

According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the number of demonstrators at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia fluctuated between 200 and 2,000 and they blocked all UN traffic through this entrance until 30 July 1989, when the Turkish-Cypriot authorities released the last two detainees.

According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the events of 19 July 1989 created considerable tension in the island and intensive efforts were made, both at the UN headquarters and at Nicosia, to contain and resolve the situation.

According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, on 21 July 1989 the UN Secretary General expressed his concern at the events that had taken place and stressed that it was vital that all parties keep in mind the purpose of the UN buffer zone as well as their responsibility to ensure that that area was not violated.
According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General urged the Turkish-Cypriot authorities to release without delay all those who had been detained.

According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, on 24 July 1989 the President of the Security Council announced that he had conveyed to the representatives of all the parties, on behalf of the members of the Council, the Council's deep concern at the tense situation created by the incidents of 19 July 1989.

According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the President of the Security Council stressed the need strictly to respect the UN buffer zone and appealed for the immediate release of all persons still detained.

According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the President of the Security Council asked all concerned to show maximum restraint and to take urgent steps that would bring about a relaxation of tension and contribute to the creation of an atmosphere favourable to the negotiations.
